title: Cherry and Bramble Race the Dark
markdown:
Cherry the chinchilla was a little puffball of fur, so soft and so fast her feet could tap-dance on a dewdrop without making a ripple. Her tail was a fluffy wonder, like a little grey cloud that bobbed when she hopped. Bramble the beagle had ears that flopped and jiggled when he ran, and his bark was a happy woof-hooray that could make even a grumpy daisy smile.

These two were the bestest of friends, and their favourite place in the whole wide world was Sunny Meadow Playground. They had a ball, a super-duper bright red bouncing ball, the best ball ever. It went boing-boing-boing, a bouncing beat.

So there they were, kicking the ball. Cherry would zoom, zoom, zoom, and Bramble would woof, woof, woof, chasing after it. They’d giggle and tumble, rolling in the soft green grass until their tummies tickled. The sun, which had been shining so bright and golden, started to stretch and yawn, getting all sleepy and painting the sky with stripes of pink and orange, like a giant rainbow popsicle.

“Oh dear,” puffed Cherry, her fluffy tail giving a little wobble. “It’s getting late.”

Bramble’s floppy ears drooped just a little. “We need to go home soon,” he woofed softly, nudging the red ball with his nose.

Then Cherry gasped, a tiny sound like a whispered breeze. “Our ball. Our super-duper bright red bouncing ball. We left it in the cubby.”

Oh no. That cubby was at the very far end of the playground, near the big slide that looked like a silver waterfall. And the sun was sinking faster than a biscuit in a mug of hot cocoa. Cherry’s whiskers twitched. A shiver ran all the way down her fluffy tail. What if they could not get it back before it was too dark? Her paws suddenly felt cold.

“We have to get it back,” Cherry squeaked.

Bramble’s tail gave a hopeful thump-thump. “We’ll race the sunset,” he declared, his voice full of beagle-y bravery.

Cherry shivered a tiny bit, pulling her fluffy tail closer. “But it’s getting a little bit dark,” she whispered. The dark always made her feel a little bit wiggly inside, like she’d eaten too many fizzy sherbet lemons. If they didn’t go right now, the playground would be swallowed by night, and their ball would be all alone. That thought was almost scarier than the dark itself.

Whoosh. Off they went.

The playground, usually so bright and cheerful, was starting to look a little shadowy. The slides seemed longer and a bit mysterious. The swings looked like sleepy giants with their chains hanging down. Cherry’s little chinchilla heart went thump-thump-thump, faster than her feet usually could. The air felt cooler, and smelled like dewy grass and sleepy flowers.

Just as they rounded the big oak tree, its leaves rustling like secrets, they heard a tiny wiggle-wiggle sound. A little earthworm, looking very confused, was wriggling in circles on the path.

“Oh dear,” said Bramble, skidding to a happy halt, tail wagging a friendly greeting. “Are you lost, little worm?”

The worm wiggled sadly, its tiny body looking a bit damp and forlorn. “I can’t find my way back to my cozy damp burrow. The path just disappeared.”

Cherry, forgetting her worry about the dark for a moment, felt a little squeeze of sympathy. “We can help. Which way did you come from?”

As they were helping the worm wiggle-waggle in the right direction, pointing out familiar pebbles and twisty roots, a chattering squirrel named Nutmeg, with a tail like a feathery question mark, scampered down a tree trunk with a frantic rustle of leaves.

“Oh, friends, have you seen a tiny shiny button? It rolled away from my nest, and it’s my favourite. It sparkles like a tiny star.” Nutmeg’s paws wrung in distress.

Cherry and Bramble looked at each other. They really, really wanted to get to their ball, but the worm and the squirrel looked so sad and worried.

“We’ll help you find it,” said Bramble, his tail giving a determined wag.

They searched under fallen leaves that crunched like crispy potato chips and behind smooth grey pebbles. Finally Cherry, with her sharp chinchilla eyes, spotted it, glinting near a bright bluebell that was just closing its petals for the night.

“Here it is,” she chirped.

Nutmeg did a happy little dance, her bushy tail swishing with joy. “Oh, thank you. Thank you. As a thank you, I know a shortcut, and my cousin, Eilir the glow-worm, lives near the cubby. He can lend you his light. He’s a very bright fellow.”

The little worm, feeling much better and safe from being stepped on, added, “And I can show you the path with the softest moss, so your little feet don’t get tired.”

A shortcut and a glow-worm’s light. This was perfect.

The sun was now just a sliver on the horizon, painting everything in a soft dusky purple, and the playground cubby seemed so far away. Cherry’s tummy did a little flip-flop. The idea of running in the fading light, when shapes began to blur and shadows grew longer, still made her feel a bit wobbly. She stopped, her little paws planted firmly on the soft moss. Maybe they should just go home. It was too dark. What if they got lost?

Bramble nudged her, his warm nose a comforting pressure. “Come on, Cherry. We’re so close. We’ll race the sunset. We have Eilir’s light now.”

So they followed Nutmeg’s shortcut, which was a bit twisty-turny but full of interesting smells of damp earth and pine needles. Then they saw him. Eilir the glow-worm, blinking his little light, sitting on a tall blade of grass.

“Hello,” he buzzed, his light like a tiny friendly lantern in the dimness. “Need a hand… or a light?”

Cherry felt a little bit better, seeing Eilir’s friendly glow. It was like a tiny star had come down to help them. They followed the worm’s mossy path, which was indeed very soft and quiet under their paws.

But when they finally reached the cubby, the sun had almost completely disappeared, like a coin dropped into a deep well. The cubby looked like a little dark cave, and their beautiful red ball was just a shadowy blur inside, almost invisible.

“Oh no,” whimpered Cherry, her fluffy tail drooping completely, looking like a sad grey comma. “It’s too dark to even see the ball. We’ll never find it.”

Bramble nudged her gently, his warm nose pressing against her side. “Don’t worry, Cherry. I have an idea.” He looked at Cherry, then at the dark cubby, then back at Cherry. “You’re super light, Cherry. Like a little feather. And I’m super strong. Hop on my back. We can go so fast, faster than ever. We’ll zoom right to it.”

Cherry’s eyes went wide. Riding on Bramble’s back? It sounded wobbly. And high up. She clutched her paws together. The ground looked so far away. She could hear the faint whoosh of the wind already, and it tickled her ears and made her fluffy tail quiver. What if he tripped? What if they both tumbled?

Bramble looked down at her with unwavering loyalty. “I promise, Cherry, I’ll be careful,” he woofed, his tail giving a hopeful thump against the ground.

But as he pushed off, he ran over a slightly uneven patch of grass, forcing him to adjust his stride, a slight wobble that made Cherry gasp and grip his fur tighter. The scent of damp earth and Bramble’s warm fur filled her senses as the world blurred around them. Boing-boing-boing went her heart, a bouncing beat.

They were back at Cherry’s house in a flash, the red ball safely tucked under Bramble’s chin like a precious prize.

“We did it,” Cherry squeaked, hopping off Bramble’s back, her legs feeling a little shaky but also strong. “We beat the sunset.”

Bramble gave a happy rumbling bark, his tail wagging so hard it shook his whole body. “And we helped our friends.”

As they sat together, their red ball nestled between them, warm from their adventure, Cherry watched Eilir’s light blink goodbye from her doorstep. The night air felt cool and soft, smelling of night-blooming jasmine. A shadow flickered across the lawn, reminding her of the dark shapes at the playground. This time, instead of her whiskers twitching nervously, Cherry simply wiggled her nose, recalling Bramble’s steady back and Eilir’s guiding light. She chirped a small confident chirp. Her fluffy tail gave a happy upright bounce. We’ll race the sunset, she thought, and the dark did not swallow the thought at all.
